newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Educated Afghans start fleeing new Islamist regime.
newsitem.headline: Educated Afghans start fleeing new Islamist regime.

text.p: Dozens of educated, middle-class people scrambled to leave Kabul at dawn on Friday, fleeing what one called a prison built by the purist Islamic Taleban militia which captured the Afghan capital a week ago.
"It's like being in jail. I want to be free," said one former ministry official as he boarded a minibus heading for the Pakistani border with his wife, son and two school-age daughters.
"I want my wife and daughters to have a decent life. They're not going to get that here," he said.

The Taleban have told women not to report to work until their jobs are reorganised to prevent contact with men. Women should remain at home and appear in public only if clad in the enveloping burqa, which covers them from head to foot.

Among others leaving on the eight-hour journey along a badly damaged road to the border were a doctor, an engineer and a woman banker. Few were willing to talk because Taleban fighters were wandering through the dusty bus station, a chaotic mix of people and horn-blaring minibuses.
"They're looking for people who worked for the former government," said one man whose brother is an officer in the ethnic Tajik militia of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

Masood withdrew to his home base in the Panjsher Valley north of Kabul as the city fell with barely a shot fired a week ago and the largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban have said they will attack him unless he surrenders.
"My brother is with him and I'm afraid they will find out and retaliate against me," said the 35-year-old man leaving with his wife and two children.
"They've been coming to Tajik houses and questioning people about their connections with Masood and I'm afraid they'll come for me. If they do, I don't know what will happen to me and my family."

A 20-year-old university student was leaving with his parents and two sisters, who also attended Kabul university, which had 18,000 students, about 8,000 of them women. It has been closed since the Taleban took the city and there has been no word on when it might re-open.
"My mother worked in a bank and my father is too ill to work. She can't go to work and she hasn't been paid, so there's no way we can live here and we'll go to relatives in Pakistan," he said.
"We don't think my sisters will be allowed to go back to the university and my parents want them to have a good education, so that's another reason we're leaving," he said.

"But most of all it's because of the way the Taleban are behaving. When they first came, we were happy because they brought peace, but we have seen them beating up women on the street and we can't live like this."
The student said he had watched while black-turbanned Taleban fighters beat up a man and his wife while they shopped because she wore only a scarf around her head, not a burqa.

"Then I was sitting with my friends outside my house when a woman with her face uncovered came to her door to call in her children. A Taleban yelled at her to go inside or he would open fire with his machine gun. This is no atmosphere to live in," he said.
The travellers said there were rumours that the Taleban were not allowing women to go beyond Jalalabad, the only major town between Kabul and the Khyber Pass, where Pakistan begins.

"I don't know if it's true, but I have left my wife behind and I'll send for her if I find it's safe for her to travel," said another former ministry official who was heading for Pakistan with a small son. "But we can't stay here. The Taleban have made life too difficult for us."

Many ordinary people are happy that the Taleban have taken Kabul, which has been battered by heavy factional fighting over the past four years. Peace has returned and the prices of essential commodities have fallen sharply.
But Kabul is more cosmopolitan than other Afghan cities and the communist government ousted in 1992 by mujahideen guerrillas after 13 years of war encouraged women to be educated and work.
The mujahideen government that took over was relatively liberal and women remained in school, university and their jobs.
Many educated Kabulis say they believe that era has ended, even though the Taleban have said women will be allowed to continue their education "in an Islamic manner".

"My father brought us to Kabul 15 years ago because he wanted my sister to have an education, which was not possible at home. We have relatives abroad and they'll help her finish her education because that won't happen here," said one young man who was taking his burqa-clad sister to Pakistan.
